summary: Dante tells of a journey through the three realms of the dead in the spring of 1300. Lost in a dark wood, he is led by the Roman poet Virgil down through Hell, a pit of ordered punishments, and up the mountain of Purgatory. Beatrice then guides him through the spheres of Paradise, and Saint Bernard takes him to the last vision. Each cantica has 33 cantos, and the whole is 14,233 lines of terza rima. The poem reads as the soul's road from sin to repentance to God.
context: Dante began the poem around 1308 and finished it about 1321, shortly before his death. He wrote it in Tuscan rather than Latin, which helped fix standard Italian. The first complete translation, into Latin prose, was made by Giovanni da Serravalle in 1416, and the first printed edition appeared at Foligno in 1472. No manuscript in Dante's hand survives, only copies. Boccaccio later added Divina to the title. The site carries Henry Wadsworth Longfellow's English version from the Standard Ebooks edition.

sources.title: The Divine Comedy, translated by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, Standard Ebooks

people.name: Dante Alighieri
people.note: Italian poet (c. 1265 to 1321) who wrote in the Tuscan vernacular.

people.name: Virgil
people.note: The Roman poet who stands for human reason and guides Dante through Hell and most of Purgatory.

people.name: Beatrice
people.note: Represents divine revelation and guides Dante from the end of Purgatory onward.

people.name: Saint Bernard of Clairvaux
people.note: Represents contemplative mysticism and guides Dante in the last cantos of Paradiso.

people.name: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
people.note: Made the English translation in the Standard Ebooks edition.

people.name: Giovanni Boccaccio
people.note: The earliest known user of the adjective Divina for the poem.

people.name: Giovanni da Serravalle
people.note: Made the first complete translation, into Latin prose, in 1416.

places.name: Florence
places.note: Dante's Florentine dialect formed the base of the poem's Tuscan and later of standard Italian.

places.name: Foligno
places.note: The first printed edition appeared here on 11 April 1472.

places.name: Konstanz
places.note: Serravalle made the first complete translation here during the Council of Constance.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.note: In Purgatorio it is dawn here when it is sunset on the mountain, a use of a spherical Earth.

ideas.title: Soul's road to God
ideas.note: Read allegorically, the three parts show the soul rejecting sin, living in penance, and rising to God.

ideas.title: Punishment fits the deed
ideas.note: Each soul gets a reward or punishment that matches what it did in life.

ideas.title: Reason, then revelation
ideas.note: Virgil stands for human reason and Beatrice for divine revelation, so Dante's guides change with his stage.

ideas.title: Vernacular as a literary language
ideas.note: Writing in Tuscan, not Latin, helped establish standard Italian.

ideas.title: Threes in the form
ideas.note: Three cantiche, 33 cantos each and interlocking three-line rhymes shape the poem.

passages.quote: Midway upon the journey of our life I found myself within a forest dark, For the straightforward pathway had been lost
“Through me the way is to the city dolent; Through me the way is to eternal dole; Through me the way among the people lost
passages.why: The inscription on the gate of Hell.

passages.quote: “There is no greater sorrow Than to be mindful of the happy time In misery, and that thy Teacher knows
Thence we came forth to rebehold the stars.

To run o’er better waters hoists its sail The little vessel of my genius now, That leaves behind itself a sea so cruel; And of that second kingdom will I sing Wherein the human spirit doth purge itself, And to ascend to heaven becometh worthy
passages.why: Purgatorio opens on a lighter sea.

passages.quote: It was the hour when the diurnal heat No more can warm the coldness of the moon, Vanquished by earth, or peradventure Saturn, When geomancers their Fortuna Major See in the orient before the dawn Rise by a path that long remains not dim, There came to me in dreams a stammering woman, Squint in her eyes, and in her feet distorted, With hands dissevered and of sallow hue
passages.why: A dream of the Siren in Purgatorio.

passages.quote: As came to Clymene, to be made certain Of that which he had heard against himself, He who makes fathers chary still to children, Even such was I, and such was I perceived By Beatrice and by the holy light That first on my account had changed its place
passages.why: Dante learns of his coming exile.

passages.quote: But now was turning my desire and will, Even as a wheel that equally is moved, The Love which moves the sun and the other stars
passages.why: The final lines of the poem.
